title: Paradise Now
full_review:
What makes someone strap explosives to his chest and blow himself up along with dozens of innocent people? This is the question explored in "Paradise Now" (Warner Independent).

Given current tensions abroad, a thoughtful film about suicide bombers might seem a precarious undertaking. Yet director Hany Abu-Assad proves he is up to the challenge.
The compelling, if provocative, movie centers on two impoverished Palestinian mechanics -- Said (Kais Nashef) and his childhood friend, Khaled (Ali Suliman) -- who are recruited for a terrorist bombing in Israel.

Abu-Assad traces the tense final hours leading up to the mission, during which the men's conflicted consciences cause them to waffle in their resolve to go through with the plot. European-educated Suha (Lubna Azabal), a pretty, secularized Muslim, argues against their planned actions.

Among the more gripping moments are a dinner scene in which Said's eyes linger lovingly on his widowed mother, knowing that it will be his last meal with her, as well as another scene involving a bus stop and a small Israeli child.

The film also captures the anguish, humiliation and despair of many Palestinians who are misled into believing that violence is their only alternative and that "death is better than inferiority." Said and Khaled are not portrayed as crazed caricatures, but as ordinary people more deluded than demonic.

By presenting them as human beings, the film attempts to understand why someone would resort to such morally indefensible measures, without justifying the intended evil. Soberly and tautly directed, the quietly terrifying "Paradise Now" allows Palestinian grievances a voice, while articulating the futility of violence.

Subtitles.

The film contains mature thematic elements and brief rough language. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
